text:
Chapter Twenty-Three


It would be a lot easier for Maggie to stomach the coming trek through the Wilds if the square mile around Hawthorn weren’t blanketed in a dense, pall-induced fog. Thankfully, Maggie hadn’t even bothered to put away her winter clothes as the seasons shifted, because the weather was so unusually chilly. She’d dug through her clothes to try to find something—anything—to wear to traipse through the Wilds. She settled on black leggings, an old long-sleeved Hawthorn shirt, and a colorful fleece she could remove when they emerged from the pall fog. She set a Hawthorn Splinters baseball cap on her head and threw her hair into a messy bun at the nape of her neck. She’d had no idea what kind of shoes to wear but finally chose a pair of neglected sneakers.


In a small backpack, she packed extra clothing, a full water bottle, enough peanut butter and jelly sandwiches and granola bars for two days of hiking, and a sample collection kit that Dr. Silva had offered them when they’d told the botanist their plan. It would keep the gloaming creeper alive until they returned to the campus to make the decoction that would counteract the confluence.


As she walked toward campus, Maggie tried not to think about what camping with Arthur would be like. Would they have to share a tent? She had spent a restless night imagining telling him the truth about Beltane next to a campfire and reaching for him in the glow of the flames. The memories she had of Beltane were made sharp by the spell fading, and it was so easy to conjure exactly how it would feel to finally kiss him again. To have his large hands roam her body in the darkness, to feel the press of him against her. She’d driven herself into a frenzy with want and need until sleep was impossible, so her hands had drifted below the band of her underwear, and she’d taken care of herself. Now, a blush crept up her neck as she drew closer to Ilex Hall.


Arthur waited for her below the hawthorn tree. Even though it was June, the air was crisp like October. Arthur wore a hunter-green fleece and a wool beanie pulled over his ears. He held two insulated mugs, and when she arrived, he handed one to her.


Maggie took a sip. It was a little creamier than she liked, but he’d known not to put in any sugar. “You made me coffee?”


Arthur shrugged. “I make one for myself every morning. It wasn’t too hard to make one for you, too.”


“How’d you know how to make it?” She took another sip.


“Oh, I bribed Edna,” he said easily. Just as Maggie was about to spiral about whether Edna would read into Arthur asking about her coffee order, he added, “I’m joking. How many times have you called Dahlia from our office and begged her to bring you a treat?”


Somehow, it was worse that he’d just been observant. “Dahlia always forgets I don’t like it sweet.”


The howling screech of a banshee echoed through the foggy air. She looked to the sky, but the beast wasn’t close by, deterred by the warding around campus. She set her pack on the picnic table and unzipped it. “We should get going,” Arthur said, watching her.


“I need to do something first.” She rifled through her carefully packed belongings. She should have put the paint on top, but she hadn’t been thinking. Well, that wasn’t true, she had been thinking. About Arthur holding her beneath the stars, about the way his kiss had melted her, about the pressure of his leg between her thighs as they’d danced. About the hours they would be spending alone together now. She looked up at him. “Take your fleece off.”


“Excuse me?” he sputtered, and she nearly laughed to see him so unmoored. He may not remember what happened on Beltane, but she could still rattle him. His eyes grew wide as she pulled the collar of her fleece to the side, revealing her collarbone and a rune painted in an ocher pigment blended with vervain.


The shock on Arthur’s face was quickly replaced with curiosity as he put his coffee mug down and leaned in to get a better look. “Oh, wow. Vintage magic,” he said as he straightened to take off his fleece, revealing a black undershirt that clung to his biceps. She’d only ever seen him in sweaters and jackets and dress shirts that he tended to wear loose. Her mouth was suddenly very dry.


Arthur picked up the pot of paint. “You just happened to have a mixture of ocher and”—he smelled the paint and grimaced at the strength of the lemony herb scent—“vervain?”


“Of course I had body paint,” she huffed. “Doesn’t everyone keep some, just in case?”


“Just in case of what? Casual monster hunting after work?”


Maggie laughed. “It’s left over from my barhopping days.” It had been a trend, for a while, to use the coppery paint as decoration for a night out. Charms were much more popular these days. They could be worn as earrings or necklaces, even belt buckles or shoelaces, but Maggie was worried something physical would fall off during their hike. “But I guess that was a little bit like monster hunting.”


Arthur grimaced, but she gave him a small smile so he would know it was a joke. Mostly. “And the vervain?” he asked.


“I grow it in a pot on my patio. Can’t be too careful this close to the Wilds,” she explained. “And the store-bought vervain powder always feels less potent, you know?”


He was looking at her with an almost reverent expression, but she wasn’t sure what she’d done to earn that. “You are a surprise, Maggie Linden,” he said quietly.


Maggie didn’t know what to do with that statement. She hated feeling this unsteady. She hated that she didn’t know what she wanted.


No, it was worse. She knew exactly what she wanted. She wanted to push Arthur Taliesin back on this picnic table and kiss him until she was dizzy. She wanted to lead him by the hand back to her apartment instead of deep into the Wilds. But she was so, so afraid. What if she let him in and he hurt her? What if she hurt him?


Her cheeks flushed, and she turned quickly back to her bag to hide how red they were. She pulled out a small notebook she used for calculations and asked Arthur, with her back still turned, “How tall are you?”


“Six two.” Arthur sat down on the picnic table bench next to her bag, looking over at her so she couldn’t hide her expression anymore. She was secretly pleased with her guessing skills. She’d have to remember to grab that list from Rodrigo’s next time she was in town since there was no reason to hunt for her mystery man anymore. Not when he was sitting right in front of her, holding the collar of his undershirt to the side to reveal a stretch of firm, smooth chest.


Maggie dipped her smallest paintbrush in the ocher. The reality of what she was about to do struck her, and she hesitated for just a moment, standing over him. She avoided looking at his face, instead focusing on that stretch of skin dotted with a few freckles. When she dared to glance up, she found him staring at her, his lips parted, and Maggie couldn’t help but remember what it was like to have those lips on hers, all-consuming. She couldn’t breathe. She couldn’t remember what she was supposed to be doing. She ached for him, a hollow need between her legs that was getting harder and harder to ignore.


“Maggie.” His voice was barely above a whisper, more growl than speech. She tore her gaze from his lips and pressed her palm to his shoulder, leaning him back against the table. He let out a low oof, and then Maggie held the brush to his skin.


“Hold still,” she commanded. She carefully dragged the paintbrush across his skin, each line and curve of the rune a precise match to the spell she’d calculated. She’d adjusted it for his height and birthday, which she’d looked up in the university celebration directory the night before. When the rune was complete, she brought her face close to his skin and blew on it to dry it quickly. Goose bumps rose along his skin, sending a thrill through Maggie.


She paused, and, almost imperceptibly, Arthur tensed and his jaw twitched. He must have realized what was coming, too. “Go on,” he breathed, and she wondered if he felt whatever this was between them like she did. Every word out of his mouth was a reminder of what he’d said on Beltane, every touch, every sound.


She placed two fingers on the rune she’d just drawn. She tried not to think about the way his skin felt beneath her fingers, about her palm still pressed against his left shoulder to keep him still, and she said the protection spell in a shaky but sure voice. A cord of light zipped through the ocher paint, and Maggie knew the spell was wrapping its way around Arthur like armor, just as it had on her that morning.


Maggie didn’t pull away immediately. She stayed between his spread legs, crouched awkwardly over his body. I’m just making sure the rune activated properly. But she could barely convince herself that was true. Before she could say or do something she would regret, she stepped backward, and the spell between them broke.


Arthur released his collar, hiding her work, and tugged the fleece back over his head. His voice was strained as he hiked his pack over his shoulder. “We need to get going. There’s a bit of a drive and then a long walk before we cross the Dismal.”



—


They didn’t say much as they walked through the first stretch of the forest. Arthur had offered to take Maggie’s bag, but she had leveled a withering glare his way, and he’d just smirked and walked on. They were on a small path that curved through the wild growth, but it was narrow and often overgrown, and the mist made it difficult to see far beyond the few feet around them. Maggie jumped at every sound, whether it was the far-off, ghastly cry of a banshee echoing through the trees or the crunch of a leaf, but Arthur moved with a practiced ease, and Maggie admired his confidence from behind.


When Maggie couldn’t stand the silence between them anymore, she called out, “You really…um…seem to know what you’re doing out here.” Above and below, what is wrong with me.


Arthur turned to look at her long enough for her to see his crooked grin. “I told you I was familiar with the Wilds.”


“I kind of assumed that was a theoretical familiarity.”


They came upon an overgrown blueberry bush blocking the path, and Arthur held the branches to the side so she could pass. “You know how my dad is a park ranger? Well, instead of letting me stay home and watch cartoons all summer, he would take me and Rory to work with him. We mostly stayed in the ranger cabin, but sometimes he’d take us scouting with him.”


Maggie’s eyes went wide. “Two little kids in the Wilds?”


Arthur laughed. “It wasn’t necessarily the best idea my dad has ever had. My mom was apoplectic when she first found out, but I loved it. So did Rory—he grew up to be a ranger, too, but he works over in Atlantia in the coastal park.”


“What about you?” Maggie asked as she held some branches aside for Arthur.


“What about me?”


“If you loved it, did you ever think about becoming a ranger?”


Arthur shrugged, a strange look on his face. “I was never going to be a park ranger. My future was always in the other family business.” Maggie wasn’t quite sure how to read the tone of his voice. It wasn’t anger, precisely, but there was a bitter edge to it. The silence dragged on for a moment. She hated how their easy conversations had become awkward again after her memories had returned.


Maggie thought about Arthur’s words in Bean There, Done That, that no one asked him many questions, assuming they knew about him. “What was it like? Growing up with Rowena?”


“You know, my mom always thought she was so different from my dad, but I went straight to her alchemy lab every day after school, and I loved that as much as my summers in the Wilds.”


Maggie couldn’t help but smile when she imagined him sitting on a too-tall stool in front of a bubbling alembic, his curious eyes magnified by his glasses, dark hair unruly.


When Arthur spoke again, he sounded thoughtful and a little sad. “My mom was brilliant. She was funny, too. Her jokes always had a bite to them, and we laughed all the time, even when things got hard at the end.” He glanced back at her and said, “But she demanded perfection. I felt like two different people for a long time. There was the kid I was when I was with my mom, and the one I was here. I don’t know. I sometimes wonder what I would have done with my life if I had been allowed to make mistakes. To take risks.”


“Is that why you studied alchemy? Because it was what she wanted?”


He huffed. “I’m not sure I could untangle that if I wanted to. I thought about doing something different, but how could I when she spent my whole life making me love alchemy?”


“What do you love about it?”


He paused for a moment. As they had walked and warmed up, he had tugged his beanie off his head, leaving his hair mussed. She wanted to smooth it back down, if only for an excuse to run her fingers through it. When he finally spoke, he was tentative, as if he was working out the answer for the first time. “I think I like that it’s never one thing. You need to master arcania, runes, incantations—it’s everything and it’s in everything.” As he went on, he grew more confident in his answer. “My mom always talked about the inherent power in transformation, and I feel that, too. But I think I also liked it because I was good at it, even when it was hard. Because when I think about an alchemical transformation, the path is clear, even if every turn is not.” He shook his head. “I don’t know if any of that made sense.”


“It did.” She understood. “Sometimes, when an incantation translation is just out of reach, I can feel the pull toward it. It’s a knot that I just need to unravel.”


They had started walking again as they talked, a clear stretch of path ahead of them, and Maggie hardly noticed the banshee screeches or growls of ghouls. Instead, she watched Arthur as he told her more about alchemy, watched as his eyes truly lit up when he talked about teaching, about helping his students understand the complicated topics he taught. There was a strange feeling in her chest.


“What about you? Were you always going to be a linguist?”


“Oh, I don’t think I knew what a linguist was until halfway through college. I just loved words. And old Diadhan romances.”


“Is romance the right word for stories about humans seduced into the wilderness by otherworldly faeries?” She nearly forgot how tenderly she’d thought of him as her head shot up to glare at him, but he had a teasing smile on his face.


“Yes,” she said with a dreamy sigh. “I found an old book of translated Diadhan myths on my grandmother’s shelf when I was eight. It was over for me. Every man since has been compared to Branagh and his midnight hair full of stars.”


“The same Branagh who kidnapped an unsuspecting woman while she hung her laundry to dry.”


She smacked his arm lightly. “Don’t you dare reduce Niamh to that! She was the heroine of that story.”


“She fell in love with her captor.”


“Shhhh,” Maggie said. “It’s an enemies-to-lovers story, Arthur.” He stopped walking and turned, an incredulous look on his face. She looked around but didn’t see what he could be looking at. When he didn’t say anything, just continued to stare, she went on. “The enemies have to do bad things to each other! Or then it’s just sorta grumpy-to-lovers…” She trailed off. “What?” she finally asked, worried. “Did I say something wrong?”


“No. Not at all.” His voice was breathy, and he continued to look at Maggie with an intensity that made her squirm. “I just…You’ve never called me Arthur before.”


“Oh. I must have…” she started to say, but she knew he was right. Somewhere along the way, she’d stopped thinking of him as Taliesin. Now he was Arthur. Her Arthur. Like he was truly her friend. “I guess I’ve gotten used to you.”


“Hmm,” was all he said in return, resuming his trek through the dense woods.

facts.fact: 出发日：他递无糖咖啡（观察所得，Edna 玩笑自撤）；她锁骨画赭石+vervain 符文要求他也画。
身体彩绘来历：barhopping 时代流行铜色符文；vervain 自家露台种的——店购效力不足。
facts.anchor: Of course I had body paint

facts.fact: 他脱衫露黑色紧身衣——她口干；他看她的眼神近乎虔诚：你真是个惊喜，Maggie Linden。
facts.anchor: You are a surprise, Maggie Linden

facts.fact: 绘符实况：按他身高生日调校（生日查自庆典名册）；吹干起鸡皮；掌压肩固定。
facts.anchor: blew on it to dry it quickly

facts.fact: 林谈童年：Barry 带他和 Rory 巡山——Rowena 气疯；野外的他与实验室的他是两个人。
facts.anchor: My mom was apoplectic when she first found out

facts.fact: Rowena 判词：聪明幽默笑话带刺、末期也一直笑——但她要求完美；他被允许犯错会怎样。
他的热爱陈述：炼金从来不是一件事（arcania/符文/咒语）；路是清楚的哪怕每个弯不是。
Branagh 之争：八岁祖母书架启蒙——此后男人都与 Branagh 比；他拆台绑架晾衣女；她 Niamh 是 heroine。
她喊出 enemies-to-lovers, Arthur——他愣住：你从来没叫过我 Arthur。
facts.anchor: You’ve never called me Arthur before

facts.fact: 她的内心更名：Her Arthur——像真正的朋友；他 Hmm 一声继续开路。
facts.anchor: I guess I’ve gotten used to you
